source.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
source.authors: Aryaman Arora; Zheng-Xuan Wu; Jacob Steinhardt; Sarah Schwettmann

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether circuits in the model’s MLP-neuron basis can be sparse and behaviorally faithful, using circuit metrics and interventions rather than the original neuron-pole audit or explanation-scoring method.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates neuron-basis circuits and reports outcomes relevant to V5. It does not measure the proportion of neurons with one or more named jobs or score neuron explanations on held-out activations. Other discussion of architectural sparsity is not a measurement of V2 or V4.
record.test_reason: The study builds circuits directly from Llama 3.1 8B and Gemma-2 MLP neurons, with no trained replacement model. It measures their faithfulness and completeness against SAE circuits on SVA, then traces and steers neuron circuits in case studies. These results bear directly on V5 using a different method from the original essay. RelP linearizes nonlinearities only for the backward pass; it is not a trained replacement, and all evaluation runs on the original model. The paper is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. Neuron-level tracing on MLP activations matches SAE-circuit performance at equal sparsity, but only when MLP activations replace MLP outputs and RelP replaces IG. Neuron circuits reproduce CLT case-study findings and can be steered. The authors acknowledge that comprehensive circuits remain too large for easy human interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates neuron-basis circuit sparsity and behavioral faithfulness using circuit tracing and interventions; it does not perform the original neuron-pole job-count audit. It uses IG and RelP for attribution. RelP uses a locally linearized replacement model for attribution, while final circuit evaluations are performed on the original model.
record.method_sensitivity: Attribution method changes performance: RelP generally outperforms IG. The paper also reports results under paired versus unpaired data and mean versus zero ablation; the unpaired zero-ablation results are described as preserving the overall findings.

fits_no_version.finding: In the addition case study, high-AUROC mod-10 neurons have automated descriptions such as numbers or dates that do not state their causal role. The same holds for the tens-digit neurons. The descriptions are simulator-selected (Choi et al.).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-based neuron descriptions can miss a neuron's causal role in a circuit; this is close to V6 but concerns causal role, not activation prediction.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306, 2026)
record.problems: The main SVA results are largely presented as plots without tabulated point values or reported uncertainty. The quantitative circuit evaluation uses four templatic SVA tasks; behavior-level case studies are selected tasks, and one circuit includes manual neuron filtering and selection. The Texas steering findings include a cluster that does not change the top prediction and a single-neuron effect observed in a majority, not all, of examples.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported outcomes for V1–V4, V6, or V7. The paper’s coarser MIB module-localization results are not neuron-basis circuit results and were not included.

untested.parts: Models of very large scale (the largest here is 9B). Behaviours beyond SVA templates and a few hand-chosen case studies. A quantitative head-to-head with CLT/transcoder attribution graphs on the same model, including how much behaviour their reconstruction error leaves unexplained.
Not tested: no neuron-pole job-share audit and no Qwen3-32B.
Not tested: no shares of interpretable neurons. Mixture-of-experts models are only mentioned in the discussion.
Architectural sparsity is offered only as a speculative explanation; no interpretable-neuron shares are measured.
Not tested systematically. There is a qualitative observation; see fits_no_version.
Not tested: the study uses existing simulator-scored descriptions but does not report score distributions.

missing.what: Edge-based neuron attribution graph result: RelP with stop-grads gives over 80% faithfulness at about 10^5 edges (10% of candidates) and Pareto-dominates IG-inp.
Unpaired SVA with zero ablation: MLP activations remain the sparsest representation and RelP still beats IG.

Additional neuron-circuit case studies: addition (ones-digit neurons are clean, tens-digit neurons noisier), multilingual antonyms (no single antonym neuron found), and user modelling (beliefs not at a fixed position).
Limitation stated by the authors: comprehensive neuron circuits contain too many neurons for humans to interpret easily.

record.verdict_notes: Peer reviewed (ICML 2026). The SVA results are plots without tabulated values or uncertainty. The SAE baselines include SAE error terms as nodes. The §5.4 text says "high completeness" although low completeness is the goal; this is likely a wording slip. The MIB results are at module level and correctly left out. The study measures circuit sufficiency, not how many neurons are interpretable, so it says nothing on V1, V2 or V4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the shares of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs; does not audit Qwen3-32B.
Gemma models are used for circuit-sparsity evaluations, not for measuring the claimed shares of interpretable neuron poles; no dense/MoE comparison or trillion-parameter scale test.
Does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Discusses architectural sparsity as a possible explanation, but does not measure the proposed change in interpretable-neuron shares or the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Tests neuron-basis circuit sparsity and faithfulness on SVA and selected case studies, not whether neuron circuits explain all model behavior or all behaviors covered by attribution graphs.
Does not test whether explanations that fit activating examples predict where neurons fire.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B base model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated circuit faithfulness and completeness over varying circuit sizes using paired SVA data and Integrated Gradients (IG-activations).
rows.measure: Circuit size at comparable faithfulness and completeness
rows.baseline: MLP outputs as the neuron representation; SAE bases are also compared
rows.value: MLP activations yield significantly smaller circuits than MLP outputs, by a factor of 100×, at comparable faithfulness and completeness; use of MLP activations significantly closes the gap with SAEs.
rows.note: The plotted curves are not numerically tabulated; the text states the 100× comparison and qualitative performance result.
rows.check: Under IG, MLP-activation neurons are 100x sparser than MLP outputs. But §5.2 says that with IG neurons are still "somewhat less sparse than SAE features". The gap only closes with RelP, so the IG result should be partial, not observed.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared MLP-activation neuron circuits with MLP-output and SAE circuits on paired SVA.
rows.measure: Circuit sparsity at comparable faithfulness and completeness
rows.baseline: MLP-output neuron circuits and SAE circuits
rows.value: MLP activations reduce circuit size by approximately 100x versus MLP outputs at comparable faithfulness and completeness; they substantially close the gap with standard 16k-width SAEs and remain competitive with SAE representations.
rows.note: The appendix reports results averaged over four SVA tasks; point values are plotted, not tabulated.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B

rows.baseline: MLP-output neuron circuits and 65k-width SAE circuits
rows.value: MLP activations remain competitive with the higher-capacity SAEs and provide substantially sparser circuits than MLP outputs.
rows.note: The appendix does not give exact point values for this comparison.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Steered groups of traced neurons by multiplying their original activations and examined the resulting next-token predictions.

conditions.value: Texas state-capitals example: Dallas → Texas → Austin
clusters of neurons from the traced circuit

rows.measure: Whether steering changes the model’s top prediction
rows.value: All clusters except the “state” cluster change the top prediction; suppressing the “Texas” cluster causes the model to output capitals of other states.
rows.note: The circuit initially contains 257 neurons; the authors manually identify 23 neurons with particularly meaningful descriptions and show their organization in six clusters.
rows.check: Keep partial, but add context. 5 of 6 clusters shift the top prediction as hypothesised. The 23 neurons were hand-picked from 257 traced neurons by their descriptions. 12 always-on neurons were manually excluded (§G.1). The result is from a single example (Dallas).

source_check.locator_found: §6.1, Fig 6: 257 traced neurons, 23 picked by hand, six clusters

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Steered the highest-attribution “say a capital” neuron, L23/N8079-, across examples.
rows.measure: Top-output change from capital to state
rows.value: The neuron can flip the top output from the capital to the state in a majority of examples.
rows.note: The paper plots probabilities for the capital, state, and original city against α, but does not report exact probability values in the text.
rows.check: This is one neuron, steered across 50 prompts, and it flips the output in a majority of them. No fraction is given in the text. It is only indirect evidence that the whole circuit explains the behaviour.

tranche.reason: A different method on the same question: neuron-basis circuits found with IG and RelP, scored by faithfulness and completeness and compared with SAE circuits. There is no original-style audit.

source_check.notes: Main SVA results are plots with no tabulated values, so the rows rest on qualitative sentences. The ~100x gap against MLP outputs is stated for Llama (IG) and Gemma-2-2B only, and the Gemma appendix does not name its attribution method. R4's 'considerably smaller circuit' sentence is the IG figure (Fig 3). The §5.4 edge count is garbled as '≈ 105' and read as 10^5.

statements.correction: Paired SVA, RelP, MLP activations: near-perfect faithfulness and completeness with ~200 neurons (§5.2, Fig 2). Unpaired SVA, IG, mean ablation (Fig 3): the MLP-activation basis needs a considerably smaller circuit than other methods. Unpaired SVA, mean ablation (Fig 4): RelP needs fewer neurons than IG. Unpaired zero ablation (App. D, Fig 8): MLP activations sparsest; RelP outperforms IG.
statements.problem: The unpaired 'considerably smaller circuit' result (R4) comes from Fig 3, which uses IG. The statement puts it under RelP attribution. The other claims match the text.

statements.correction: Gemma-2-2B (E.1): circuit sizes reduced by about 100x against MLP outputs at comparable faithfulness and completeness. Close to 16k SAEs, competitive with 65k SAEs. Gemma-2-9B (E.2, 16k SAEs only): 'substantially sparser' than MLP outputs, competitive with SAEs. No factor given.
statements.problem: The statement gives 'about 100x sparser' for both Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B. The text states ~100x only for Gemma-2-2B (E.1). For Gemma-2-9B it says only 'substantially/significantly sparser'. The R5–R7 descriptions are right.

statements.correction: §5.2: under IG, neurons are 'somewhat less sparse than SAE features'. §5.4, Fig 5: RelP with stop-grads reaches over 80% faithfulness with ≈10^5 edges. Limitations: 'too many neurons in a reasonably comprehensive circuit' for a human 'to easily interpret'.
statements.problem: Only the 2601.22594 part was checked. The IG and edge numbers are right (edge count garbled as '≈ 105', read as 10^5). The limitation is overstated: the text says too many neurons for a human to 'easily' interpret, not that a human cannot interpret them.

statements.correction: Appendix E (Gemma-2-2B, R5, R6) applies 'the same evaluation framework' and does not name the attribution method. RelP is specified only for the Llama 3.1 8B rows R2–R4. R1 (Llama, IG) gives the ~100x gap against MLP outputs.
statements.problem: The Gemma-2-2B side (about 100x, competitive with 16k and 65k SAEs, observed) is right. But differences_stated says the 2601.22594 rows specify RelP attribution. The cited Gemma rows (R5, R6) and Appendix E state no attribution method, and R1 uses IG.

statements.correction: Limitations: 'too many neurons in a reasonably comprehensive circuit' for a human 'to easily interpret'. §6.1: 257 traced neurons; 23 with meaningful descriptions picked by hand.
statements.problem: The statement drops 'easily': the authors say a reasonably comprehensive circuit has too many neurons for a human to easily interpret, not that a human cannot interpret it. The 23 of 257 figure is right.

statements.correction: Gemma-2-2B: ~100x sparser than MLP outputs, competitive with 16k and 65k SAEs. Gemma-2-9B (16k SAEs only): substantially sparser, competitive, no factor given. Unpaired: MLP activations sparsest under IG (Fig 3); RelP needs fewer neurons than IG (Fig 4).
statements.problem: The text gives 'about 100x' only for Gemma-2-2B, but this applies it to both 2B and 9B. 65k SAEs were used only on 2B. R4 is cited as unpaired backing for the RelP ~200-neuron result, but R4's sentence is the IG figure (Fig 3). The rest is right.
